questions.stem: About the layers of the heart wall:

options.label: A
options.text: The endocardium is lined by simple squamous epithelium

options.label: B
options.text: Purkinje fibres run in the subendocardial connective tissue

options.label: C
options.text: Cardiac muscle cells of the myocardium are arranged in a spiral fashion

options.label: D
options.text: The epicardium is the parietal layer of the serous pericardium

options.label: E
options.text: Coronary vessels and adipose tissue lie beneath the epicardial mesothelium

notes.A: Endothelium is a simple squamous lining that provides a smooth interface with blood in cardiac chambers.
notes.B: Large glycogen-rich Purkinje cells conduct impulses rapidly through connective tissue beneath ventricular endocardium.
notes.C: Helical myocardial fibre organisation helps coordinate ventricular shortening, wall thickening and twisting during contraction.
notes.D: Epicardium is the visceral serous pericardium; parietal serous pericardium lines the fibrous pericardial sac.
notes.E: Coronary arteries, veins and variable adipose deposits occupy connective tissue beneath the epicardial mesothelium.

questions.why: The endocardium lines cardiac chambers, myocardium generates contractile force, and epicardium covers the external surface. Subendocardial conduction fibres and subepicardial coronary vessels occupy distinct connective-tissue compartments.

questions.stem: About the heart valves and conducting tissue:

options.label: A
options.text: The right atrioventricular valve has three cusps

options.label: B
options.text: The aortic and pulmonary semilunar valves each have two cusps

options.label: C
options.text: The SA node lies in the superior wall of the right atrium near the SVC opening

options.label: D
options.text: The bundle of His passes from the AV node into the interventricular septum

options.label: E
options.text: Purkinje fibres are small, thin cardiac muscle cells

notes.A: The right atrioventricular valve normally comprises anterior, posterior and septal leaflets attached to the fibrous skeleton.
notes.B: Each semilunar valve normally has three cusps; a bicuspid aortic valve is a congenital variant.
notes.C: The sinoatrial node occupies the right atrial region close to the superior vena caval junction.
notes.D: The atrioventricular bundle penetrates the fibrous skeleton and divides into branches within the interventricular septal region.
notes.E: Purkinje cells are enlarged specialised cardiomyocytes with glycogen-rich cytoplasm and relatively few peripheral contractile myofibrils.

questions.why: Heart valves direct flow passively according to pressure differences, whereas specialised cardiomyocytes generate and conduct electrical impulses. Purkinje cells are conspicuously large and pale because of abundant glycogen and relatively sparse myofibrils.

questions.stem: The autonomic nerves to the heart:

options.label: A
options.text: modulate the heart rate but do not initiate it

options.label: B
options.text: initiate each heartbeat through the vagus nerves

options.label: C
options.text: reach the heart only from lower thoracic segments

options.label: D
options.text: are purely sympathetic, with no vagal supply

options.label: E
options.text: are absent from the atria and the conducting system

questions.why: Sinoatrial pacemaker cells generate spontaneous depolarisations independently of extrinsic nerves. Sympathetic and parasympathetic inputs modify pacemaker rate and conduction, while sympathetic activity also influences myocardial contractility.

notes.B: Vagal activity slows sinoatrial firing and atrioventricular conduction; it does not normally initiate each heartbeat.
notes.C: Cardiac sympathetic preganglionic neurons arise mainly from upper thoracic spinal segments and relay through sympathetic ganglia.
notes.D: Parasympathetic fibres reach the heart through vagal branches alongside sympathetic fibres in the cardiac plexus.
notes.E: Both autonomic divisions innervate nodal tissue and atrial myocardium, allowing modulation of rhythm and conduction.

questions.stem: Muscular (distributing) arteries:

options.label: A
options.text: include most of the named arteries of the body

options.label: B
options.text: have more elastin and less smooth muscle in the media than elastic arteries

options.label: C
options.text: show a prominent internal elastic lamina

options.label: D
options.text: may have an external elastic lamina at the media–adventitia boundary

notes.A: Many named peripheral distributing arteries, including radial and femoral arteries, belong to the muscular category.
notes.B: Their media contains proportionally more smooth muscle and fewer elastic lamellae than elastic conducting arteries.
notes.C: The internal elastic lamina typically appears as a distinct wavy sheet bordering the innermost medial smooth muscle.
notes.D: Larger muscular arteries may have an external elastic lamina separating the media from surrounding adventitia.
notes.E: Walls of sufficiently large muscular arteries receive adventitial and outer medial nourishment from vasa vasorum.

questions.why: Muscular arteries distribute blood through a predominantly smooth-muscle tunica media, permitting adjustment of vessel calibre. A prominent internal elastic lamina separates intima from media, and larger examples may possess an external elastic lamina.

questions.stem: The fenestrated membranes found in the tunica media are characteristic of:
questions.why: Elastic arteries contain numerous concentric fenestrated elastic lamellae throughout their tunica media. These sheets stretch during systole and recoil during diastole, helping maintain blood flow between ventricular ejections.

notes.A: Muscular arteries have predominantly smooth-muscle media bounded by distinct elastic laminae rather than numerous medial elastic sheets.
notes.C: Arterioles possess only a few smooth-muscle layers and lack the repeated medial elastic lamellae characteristic of the aorta.
notes.D: Medium veins have relatively thin smooth-muscle media with connective tissue rather than numerous concentric elastic lamellae.
notes.E: Metarterioles in classical microvascular models have discontinuous smooth-muscle coverage, not thick repeated elastic sheets.

questions.stem: A vessel whose wall thickness about equals its luminal diameter, with one or two smooth muscle layers, is most likely:
questions.why: Arterioles typically have one or two circumferential smooth-muscle layers surrounding a narrow endothelial lumen. Their high wall-to-lumen ratio and ability to change calibre support regulation of resistance and local capillary perfusion.

notes.A: Small arteries generally possess several concentric smooth-muscle layers rather than the one or two specified in this section.
notes.B: Classical metarterioles have discontinuous smooth-muscle coverage instead of the continuous circumferential coat typical of arterioles.
notes.D: Capillaries consist chiefly of endothelium and basal lamina, with possible pericytes rather than a continuous muscular coat.
notes.E: Postcapillary venules have thin endothelial walls with pericytes and relatively wide lumina, rather than concentric smooth-muscle layers.

questions.stem: Capillaries are classified mainly according to:

options.label: B
options.text: the number of pericytes around them

options.label: C
options.text: the organ and tissue that they supply

questions.why: Capillary classification depends chiefly on endothelial continuity, fenestrations and basal lamina organisation. Continuous, fenestrated and discontinuous capillaries have different permeability properties suited to the exchange requirements of their tissues.

notes.A: Diameter and length vary with tissue and preparation, but endothelial architecture provides the principal histological classification.
notes.B: Pericyte coverage varies between microvascular beds but does not define the three conventional endothelial capillary categories.
notes.C: Organ distribution helps predict capillary type, but structural classification depends on the endothelial and basal lamina characteristics.
notes.E: Capillaries lack the separate thick adventitial coat of larger vessels, so adventitial thickness cannot distinguish these categories.

questions.stem: The diaphragm across a capillary fenestration is thought to derive from:

options.label: E
options.text: the glycocalyx of a pinocytotic vesicle

questions.why: It comes from glycocalyx once enclosed in the vesicle that formed the fenestration.

questions.stem: Pericytes are regulated mainly by:
questions.why: Pericytes are contractile and respond to endothelial NO.

notes.D: A local mediator but not the stated control.
notes.E: Circulating hormone, not the stated control.

questions.stem: Which layer is thickest in the wall of a large vein?
questions.why: Large veins such as the vena cava have a relatively thin tunica media and a prominent adventitia containing collagen and longitudinal smooth-muscle bundles. This outer coat provides mechanical support to a large, compliant lumen.

notes.A: The intima forms the endothelial and subendothelial lining but is considerably thinner than the prominent outer coat.
notes.C: Large veins possess relatively little circumferential medial muscle compared with the longitudinal bundles in their thick adventitia.
notes.D: An internal elastic lamina is generally inconspicuous in large veins and does not constitute their thickest wall layer.
notes.E: Subendothelial connective tissue belongs to the intima and does not provide the extensive longitudinal muscular outer coat.

questions.stem: Atypical blood vessels:

options.label: A
options.text: Coronary arteries are classed as medium-sized muscular arteries

options.label: B
options.text: Coronary artery walls are thinner than comparable limb arteries

options.label: C
options.text: Dural venous sinuses are lined by endothelium and lack smooth muscle

options.label: D
options.text: The great saphenous vein has a thick circular muscle coat in its media

options.label: E
options.text: The great saphenous vein has a well-developed internal elastic membrane

notes.B: THICKER, due to more circular smooth muscle.
notes.E: It is thin and poorly developed.

questions.why: False: B, E. THICKER, due to more circular smooth muscle. It is thin and poorly developed.

questions.stem: Atherosclerosis in the coronary arteries restricting oxygen supply to the myocardium leads to:
questions.why: Coronary atherosclerotic plaques can restrict coronary blood flow or precipitate thrombosis, reducing oxygen delivery relative to myocardial demand. This produces ischaemic heart disease, including angina or myocardial infarction depending on severity and duration.

notes.A: Dural sinus thrombosis obstructs cerebral venous drainage rather than directly restricting arterial oxygen delivery to cardiac muscle.
notes.B: Varicose veins arise from abnormalities of superficial venous walls and valves, rather than atherosclerotic narrowing of coronary arteries.
notes.D: Lymphoedema results from impaired lymphatic drainage and interstitial fluid accumulation, rather than coronary arterial insufficiency.
notes.E: Pulmonary hypertension affects pressure within the pulmonary circulation, whereas coronary atherosclerosis primarily compromises blood supply to myocardium.

questions.stem: Which vessel normally has 3–10 layers of smooth muscle and no vasa vasorum?
questions.why: Small arteries commonly have several circumferential smooth-muscle layers, more than typical arterioles, but relatively thin walls nourished by diffusion. They regulate distribution and resistance before blood enters the arteriolar microcirculation.

notes.A: Elastic arteries contain numerous medial elastic lamellae and require vasa vasorum to nourish their thick outer walls.
notes.B: Larger distributing muscular arteries often possess many more medial smooth-muscle layers and may contain vasa vasorum.
notes.C: Large veins have a prominent adventitia and may contain vasa vasorum, rather than the specified small muscular arterial architecture.
notes.E: Typical arterioles contain one or two smooth-muscle layers, fewer than the three to ten described in this question.

questions.stem: The vessel described as the major determinant of systemic blood pressure is the:
questions.why: Arterioles are major adjustable resistance vessels because their small luminal radius changes substantially with smooth-muscle contraction or relaxation. Altering arteriolar resistance helps regulate systemic arterial pressure and distribution of tissue blood flow.

notes.A: Elastic arteries primarily buffer pulsatile ventricular ejection through elastic expansion and recoil, rather than providing the main adjustable peripheral resistance.
notes.B: Muscular distributing arteries can regulate flow but smaller resistance vessels exert especially important control over systemic vascular resistance.
notes.C: Capillaries provide extensive exchange area and lack continuous smooth-muscle coats capable of active arteriolar calibre regulation.
notes.D: Medium veins function mainly as capacitance and return vessels, rather than being the principal adjustable systemic resistance site.

questions.stem: Which layer of the heart wall contains the Purkinje fibres?
questions.why: Purkinje fibres form specialised ventricular conducting networks chiefly within subendocardial connective tissue. Their large glycogen-rich cells contain sparse peripheral myofibrils and rapidly distribute electrical activation to neighbouring contractile ventricular myocardium.

notes.B: The subepicardial layer contains coronary vessels, nerves and adipose tissue rather than the principal ventricular Purkinje network.
notes.C: The middle myocardium predominantly consists of contractile cardiomyocytes, although terminal conducting fibres communicate with deeper myocardial cells.
notes.D: The fibrous skeleton supports valves and electrically separates atrial and ventricular myocardium, rather than housing most Purkinje fibres.
notes.E: Visceral serous pericardium forms the epicardium on the external cardiac surface, opposite the principal subendocardial conduction network.

questions.stem: The coronary vessels and most of the cardiac adipose tissue lie in the:
questions.why: The epicardium consists of mesothelium and underlying connective tissue that often contains substantial fat. Major coronary vessels travel within this subepicardial compartment before distributing smaller branches into the underlying myocardium.

notes.A: Subendocardial connective tissue contains ventricular Purkinje fibres and smaller vessels rather than most epicardial coronary vessels and fat.
notes.C: Endocardial endothelium is a thin luminal cell layer and does not accommodate large coronary vessels or adipose deposits.
notes.D: Contractile myocardium contains an extensive capillary network, while major surface coronary vessels and fat chiefly occupy the epicardium.
notes.E: Fibrous pericardium forms the external protective sac rather than the connective tissue directly associated with epicardial coronary vessels.

questions.stem: Compared with ordinary cardiac muscle cells, Purkinje fibres are:

options.label: A
options.text: smaller and darker, with more myofibrils

options.label: B
options.text: thinner, with central rows of nuclei

options.label: C
options.text: larger and paler, with fewer myofibrils

questions.why: Purkinje fibres are modified cardiomyocytes specialised for rapid impulse conduction rather than force generation. Their abundant glycogen and relatively sparse peripheral myofibrils produce a characteristic large, pale appearance in routine histological sections.

notes.A: Ordinary contractile cardiomyocytes contain abundant myofibrils and stain more intensely than the larger glycogen-rich Purkinje cells.
notes.B: Purkinje cells are relatively large and may contain central nuclei, rather than forming slender multinucleated rows of ordinary fibres.
notes.D: Purkinje cells maintain intercellular junctions supporting rapid electrical coupling, rather than lacking junctional connections between conducting cells.
notes.E: Purkinje fibres retain a modified cardiac muscle identity and are not spindle-shaped cells resembling ordinary smooth muscle.

questions.stem: Which feature best identifies an elastic artery in a section stained for elastin?

options.label: A
options.text: A single wavy internal elastic lamina

options.label: B
options.text: An adventitia thicker than the media

options.label: C
options.text: Longitudinal smooth muscle in the adventitia

questions.why: Multiple concentric fenestrated elastic lamellae throughout a thick tunica media identify an elastic conducting artery. These lamellae store energy during systolic expansion and return it through recoil during diastole.

notes.A: A single conspicuous internal elastic lamina is particularly characteristic of a muscular artery with a smooth-muscle-dominant media.
notes.B: An adventitia substantially thicker than the media is characteristic of many large veins, rather than a typical elastic artery.
notes.C: Prominent longitudinal adventitial smooth-muscle bundles suggest large veins such as the vena cava rather than an elastic arterial wall.
notes.E: Intimal valves are typical of many medium veins and do not identify an elastic artery such as the aorta.

questions.stem: In a muscular artery, the most prominent elastic structure is the:
questions.why: The internal elastic lamina forms a distinct elastic sheet between the intima and smooth-muscle media of muscular arteries. Its wavy appearance in sections reflects the elastic architecture and contraction or preparation of the vessel wall.

notes.A: An external elastic lamina may be visible in larger muscular arteries, but the internal lamina is typically more conspicuous.
notes.B: Numerous repeated fenestrated elastic lamellae throughout the media characterise elastic arteries rather than typical muscular distributing arteries.
notes.C: Adventitial elastic fibres contribute to connective-tissue support but do not usually form the prominent boundary separating intima and media.
notes.D: Subendothelial connective tissue may contain elastic components, but the distinct internal elastic lamina forms the characteristic visible medial boundary.

questions.stem: The vasa vasorum supply:

options.label: A
options.text: the outer wall of large vessels

questions.why: Vasa vasorum are small vessels that nourish the adventitia and outer media of sufficiently large blood vessels. Their presence compensates for limited diffusion of oxygen and nutrients from the main vessel lumen through a thick wall.

notes.B: Capillary endothelial cells obtain nutrients directly from luminal blood and surrounding tissue, without a separate network of wall vessels.
notes.C: Arteriolar walls are sufficiently thin for diffusion from blood and neighbouring tissue, rather than requiring a separate intimal blood supply.
notes.D: Venous valves are thin endothelial-covered connective-tissue folds and do not generally require their own extensive vasa vasorum network.
notes.E: Small arterial walls can receive nutrients by diffusion; vasa vasorum become especially important in thicker walls of large vessels.

questions.stem: Blood bypasses a capillary bed through the thoroughfare channel when:
questions.why: In the classical metarteriole model, precapillary sphincter contraction restricts entry into individual capillaries. Blood can then continue through a thoroughfare pathway towards a venule, although real microvascular architecture varies substantially between tissues.

notes.A: Pericytes can influence microvascular function, but the classical routing mechanism described depends on contraction of precapillary sphincters.
notes.C: Postcapillary venular constriction increases downstream resistance and may raise capillary pressure rather than selectively closing precapillary entrances.
notes.D: Closing an arteriovenous shunt restricts that alternative pathway; the classical thoroughfare mechanism instead bypasses capillaries through upstream sphincter closure.
notes.E: Capillary endothelium lacks a conventional circular sphincter muscle coat and does not itself provide the classic precapillary valve mechanism.

questions.stem: Which capillary type allows only small molecules to pass, mainly by pinocytotic transport?
questions.why: Continuous capillaries have tight junctions and an intact basal lamina.

questions.stem: Capillaries of the brain differ from other continuous capillaries in that they:

options.label: B
options.text: have wide gaps between endothelial cells

options.label: E
options.text: have Kupffer cells in their walls

questions.why: Brain continuous capillaries possess highly restrictive endothelial tight junctions, very low nonspecific transcytosis and a continuous basal lamina. These features, supported by pericytes and astrocytic signals, contribute to selective blood–brain barrier permeability.

notes.A: Diaphragm-free fenestrations characterise glomerular capillary endothelium, not the usual restrictive endothelial structure of brain capillaries.
notes.B: Wide endothelial gaps would increase uncontrolled permeability, whereas brain capillary junctions strongly restrict paracellular passage.
notes.C: Brain capillaries possess basal laminae associated with endothelial cells and pericytes rather than completely lacking extracellular matrix support.
notes.E: Kupffer cells are resident hepatic macrophages associated with sinusoids, not characteristic structural cells of the brain endothelial barrier.

questions.stem: The glomerulus of the kidney contains capillaries that are:
questions.why: Glomerular endothelial cells contain numerous fenestrations that generally lack diaphragms. The endothelial glycocalyx, thick shared glomerular basement membrane and podocyte filtration slit structures together permit rapid plasma filtration while restricting cells and most proteins.

notes.A: Continuous nonfenestrated endothelium is characteristic of many other tissues and does not provide the typical glomerular filtration architecture.
notes.B: Kupffer cells are hepatic macrophages associated with liver sinusoids, rather than components of the normal glomerular capillary wall.
notes.C: Glomerular capillaries have a prominent specialised basement membrane despite endothelial fenestrations, unlike discontinuous sinusoidal vascular arrangements.
notes.D: Glomerular capillary endothelium is fenestrated, and mesangial cells provide specialised support rather than making it a continuous capillary bed.

questions.stem: Kupffer cells are found in the sinusoids of the:
questions.why: Kupffer cells are resident macrophages positioned along hepatic sinusoidal lumina. They phagocytose blood-borne particles, microorganisms and cellular debris, supporting immune surveillance of blood arriving through the hepatic portal and arterial circulations.

notes.B: Splenic red pulp contains macrophages that remove damaged erythrocytes, but these are not conventionally named Kupffer cells.
notes.C: Bone marrow contains macrophages associated with haematopoietic cells and sinusoids, rather than the liver-specific resident Kupffer population.
notes.D: Adrenal medullary vascular spaces deliver secreted catecholamines, but their associated immune cells are not specifically termed Kupffer cells.
notes.E: Pituitary endocrine tissue has fenestrated capillaries facilitating hormone exchange, rather than hepatic sinusoids containing Kupffer cells.

questions.stem: Ito (stellate) cells in the liver are specialised to:
questions.why: Hepatic stellate cells occupy the space of Disse between hepatocytes and sinusoidal endothelium. In their quiescent state they store retinoids in lipid droplets; after injury they can become matrix-producing cells contributing to hepatic fibrosis.

notes.A: Kupffer cells and splenic macrophages remove cellular debris and erythrocytes, whereas quiescent hepatic stellate cells specialise in retinoid storage.
notes.C: Hepatocytes synthesise bile acids from cholesterol, rather than hepatic stellate cells providing the principal bile acid biosynthetic pathway.
notes.D: Albumin is synthesised primarily by hepatocytes and secreted into blood, rather than being the characteristic product of quiescent stellate cells.
notes.E: Sinusoidal endothelial cells form the vascular lining; stellate cells occupy the adjacent perisinusoidal space of Disse.

questions.stem: Oedema in acute inflammation results mainly from leakage at the:
questions.why: Postcapillary venules are important sites of acute inflammatory permeability changes and leukocyte extravasation. Mediators such as histamine alter endothelial junctions, increasing protein-rich fluid escape into interstitial tissue and contributing to oedema.

notes.A: Arterioles dilate to increase local perfusion during inflammation, but postcapillary venules are characteristic sites of mediator-induced permeability increases.
notes.B: Metarterioles in classical models regulate microvascular distribution, rather than providing the primary site of acute inflammatory plasma leakage.
notes.D: Muscular arteries have thicker walls and are not the usual site of rapid histamine-associated endothelial gap formation.
notes.E: Lymphatic capillaries remove excess interstitial fluid and proteins; their limited drainage may worsen oedema but is not the specified leakage source.

questions.stem: Valves in veins are formed by folds of the:
questions.why: Venous valves consist of paired folds of tunica intima containing connective-tissue cores covered by endothelium. Their orientation permits forward venous flow while limiting retrograde movement, particularly in limb veins exposed to gravitational pressure.

notes.A: The tunica media contains smooth muscle, whereas venous valve leaflets arise as endothelial-covered folds of the intimal layer.
notes.B: Adventitia provides external connective-tissue support and does not project into the lumen as the characteristic valve leaflets.
notes.C: A distinct external elastic lamina is generally inconspicuous in veins and is not the tissue layer forming venous valves.
notes.E: Vasa vasorum nourish thicker vessel walls, rather than forming the intraluminal endothelial folds preventing retrograde venous flow.

questions.stem: Which vessel has the thinnest wall relative to the size of its lumen?
questions.why: Medium veins generally have wider lumina and thinner walls relative to lumen diameter than corresponding arteries. Their lower intravascular pressures permit a relatively thin media and compliant architecture suited to blood storage and return.

notes.A: Muscular arteries have prominent circumferential smooth-muscle media adapted to arterial pressures and therefore relatively thick walls.
notes.B: Arterioles have narrow lumina surrounded by smooth muscle, making their wall thickness relatively substantial compared with lumen diameter.
notes.C: Elastic arteries possess thick media containing multiple elastic lamellae, unlike the relatively thin walls of comparable venous vessels.
notes.D: Small arteries possess several medial smooth-muscle layers that are relatively thick compared with their smaller luminal diameter.

questions.stem: A vessel shows a large lumen and a thick adventitia with longitudinal bundles of smooth muscle. It is most likely the:
questions.why: The inferior vena cava is a large vein with a prominent adventitia containing longitudinal smooth-muscle bundles. Its wide lumen and relatively thin media contrast with the thick elastic or muscular media of arteries.

notes.B: The aorta is an elastic artery whose thick media contains many concentric elastic lamellae, rather than prominent venous adventitial muscle.
notes.C: The femoral artery has a substantial circumferential smooth-muscle media and prominent elastic boundaries, unlike the described large venous architecture.
notes.D: The popliteal vein is a medium vein with a less characteristic longitudinal muscular adventitia than the inferior vena cava.
notes.E: Coronary arteries are muscular arteries with prominent medial smooth muscle, rather than the characteristic longitudinal bundles of large venous adventitia.

questions.stem: The great saphenous vein is unusual because it has a:

options.label: A
options.text: fenestrated elastic membrane in the media

options.label: B
options.text: thick, circular muscle coat in the media

questions.why: The great saphenous vein commonly exhibits a relatively substantial circumferential smooth-muscle media compared with many veins. Its muscular wall contributes to regulation of calibre and adaptation to haemodynamic loading in the dependent lower limb.

notes.A: Numerous fenestrated medial elastic lamellae are characteristic of elastic arteries, not the usual muscular architecture of the great saphenous vein.
notes.C: The internal elastic lamina of veins is generally less distinct than that of muscular arteries, rather than the defining unusual feature here.
notes.D: The great saphenous vein retains an endothelial luminal lining, as do other normal blood vessels in the systemic circulation.
notes.E: Its adventitia contains collagenous connective tissue providing structural support, rather than being devoid of the principal extracellular matrix fibre.

questions.stem: The dural venous sinuses are best described as:

options.label: B
options.text: muscular veins with an elastic lamina

questions.why: Dural venous sinuses are endothelial-lined channels formed between layers of cranial dura mater. Their rigid connective-tissue boundaries lack a typical muscular venous wall and valves, permitting drainage of cerebral venous blood.

notes.A: Dural sinuses lack ordinary venous valves and do not possess the thick muscular walls described in this alternative.
notes.B: Their walls are formed by dural connective tissue lined by endothelium rather than a conventional smooth-muscle media and elastic lamina.
notes.D: Dural venous sinuses carry venous blood; meningeal lymphatic vessels are distinct structures involved in lymphatic drainage.
notes.E: The sinuses are relatively large venous collecting channels, rather than microscopic networks mediating capillary exchange within meningeal tissue.

questions.stem: Lymphatic capillaries differ from blood capillaries in that they:

options.label: A
options.text: have a thick basal lamina and pericytes

options.label: B
options.text: carry red cells and platelets in lymph

options.label: D
options.text: begin blindly with a patchy basal lamina

questions.why: Initial lymphatic capillaries begin blindly and contain overlapping endothelial cells with discontinuous or poorly developed basal lamina. Anchoring filaments help maintain openings for uptake of excess interstitial fluid, proteins and other material.

notes.A: Initial lymphatic capillaries generally lack continuous basal lamina and pericyte coverage, facilitating entry of interstitial fluid and macromolecules.
notes.B: Normal lymph contains immune cells but few erythrocytes or platelets, rather than carrying the usual cellular composition of blood.
notes.C: Lymphatic capillaries are lined by a single endothelial layer with specialised overlapping junctions, not stratified epithelium.
notes.E: Diaphragm-covered fenestrations characterise certain blood capillaries; initial lymphatics instead admit fluid through specialised overlapping endothelial junctions.

questions.stem: The atrioventricular bundle (of His) runs into the:
questions.why: The atrioventricular bundle penetrates the central fibrous body from the AV node and reaches the upper interventricular septum. It divides into right and left bundle branches that distribute impulses towards ventricular Purkinje networks.

notes.A: The atrioventricular node lies near the inferior interatrial septal region, but its conducting bundle proceeds into the interventricular septum.
notes.B: The crista terminalis is a right atrial muscular ridge rather than the principal pathway of the atrioventricular bundle.
notes.C: The coronary sinus drains cardiac veins and lies near the AV nodal region, rather than housing the descending ventricular conduction bundle.
notes.D: Purkinje networks distribute impulses to papillary muscles and ventricular myocardium downstream of the bundle's division within the septum.

questions.stem: Which is listed as a function of the blood vascular system?

options.label: A
options.text: Circulating hormones to their target cells

options.label: B
options.text: Producing red cells in the vessel walls

options.label: C
options.text: Filtering lymph before it enters veins

options.label: D
options.text: Storing vitamin A in the vessel walls

questions.why: Blood vessels distribute hormones from endocrine sources to distant responsive tissues, alongside transporting respiratory gases, nutrients and metabolic wastes. Circulation thus integrates organ functions through both substance delivery and chemical signalling.

notes.B: Adult erythrocyte production occurs chiefly in red bone marrow, not within the walls of ordinary blood vessels.
notes.C: Lymph nodes filter lymph before it returns to the bloodstream, rather than the blood vascular system performing this specialised function.
notes.D: Hepatic stellate cells store vitamin A in lipid droplets, rather than vascular walls serving as the principal retinoid reservoir.
notes.E: Hepatocytes secrete bile into canaliculi and the biliary tract, rather than normally releasing bile into circulating blood.

questions.stem: The epithelium of the endocardium is:
questions.why: Endocardial endothelium is a single layer of flattened squamous cells continuous with vascular endothelium. It forms a smooth, low-friction blood-contacting surface over subendothelial connective tissue.

notes.A: Simple cuboidal epithelium commonly lines small ducts and renal tubules, rather than the flattened endothelial lining of cardiac chambers.
notes.C: Stratified squamous epithelium protects surfaces against abrasion and is not the normal blood-contacting lining of the heart.
notes.D: Pseudostratified columnar epithelium commonly lines conducting respiratory passages rather than the inner surfaces of cardiac chambers.
notes.E: Transitional epithelium accommodates distension in urinary passages, not the normal endothelial surface of the heart.

questions.stem: The cardiac muscle cells of the myocardium are arranged:

options.label: E
options.text: as inner circular and outer longitudinal coats

questions.why: Ventricular cardiomyocytes form interconnected bundles whose orientation changes across myocardial depth, creating a complex helical architecture. This arrangement supports ventricular twisting, wall thickening and efficient ejection during systole.

notes.A: The myocardium contains multiple interconnected fibre orientations rather than one simple circumferential layer around each chamber.
notes.B: Myocardial fibres have varying orientations across the wall and are not arranged exclusively in parallel longitudinal sheets.
notes.D: Cardiomyocytes form organised interconnected networks through intercalated discs, rather than isolated randomly oriented contractile bundles.
notes.E: Distinct inner circular and outer longitudinal coats characterise much gastrointestinal smooth muscle, rather than the complex helical cardiac myocardium.

questions.stem: Veins and nerves of the heart wall, along with the Purkinje fibres, lie in the:
questions.why: The subendocardium contains connective tissue, small vessels, nerves and specialised ventricular Purkinje fibres. It links the chamber lining with underlying contractile myocardium and supports distribution of impulses into ventricular muscle.

notes.A: Endocardial endothelium is a single flattened cellular layer, rather than the connective-tissue compartment containing large specialised conducting cells.
notes.B: The middle myocardium is predominantly contractile cardiac muscle, whereas the major Purkinje network lies in subendocardial connective tissue.
notes.C: Epicardial mesothelium covers the external heart surface and is separated from the subendocardial ventricular conduction network.
notes.E: Fibrous pericardium encloses the heart externally rather than supporting Purkinje fibres adjacent to the ventricular luminal lining.

questions.stem: The bicuspid (mitral) valve guards the:
questions.why: The mitral valve separates the left atrium and left ventricle and has anterior and posterior leaflets. It opens during ventricular filling and closes when ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure.

notes.A: The right atrioventricular opening is guarded by the tricuspid valve, which normally has three major leaflets.
notes.B: The aortic orifice is guarded by the aortic semilunar valve, which controls left ventricular outflow into the aorta.
notes.C: The pulmonary orifice is guarded by a semilunar valve controlling right ventricular outflow, rather than by the mitral valve.
notes.D: The coronary sinus opening drains myocardial venous blood into the right atrium and is not the left atrioventricular opening.

questions.stem: The SA node lies in the:

options.label: A
options.text: right atrial wall near the SVC opening

options.label: B
options.text: interatrial septum near the coronary sinus

options.label: D
options.text: left atrial wall near the pulmonary veins

options.label: E
options.text: muscular septum near the cardiac apex

questions.why: The sinoatrial node is located near the junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium, typically within subepicardial connective tissue. Its specialised pacemaker cardiomyocytes spontaneously initiate normal sinus rhythm.

notes.B: The atrioventricular node lies near the inferior interatrial septum and coronary sinus opening, rather than the sinoatrial node.
notes.C: The atrioventricular bundle enters the upper ventricular septal region, rather than the principal atrial pacemaker being located there.
notes.D: The normal sinoatrial node lies in the right atrium near the superior vena cava, not beside left atrial pulmonary veins.
notes.E: The cardiac apex contains ventricular myocardium and distal conducting networks, rather than the usual anatomical site of the sinoatrial node.

questions.stem: Arterioles have a diameter of about:
questions.why: Arterioles are small resistance vessels commonly described as approximately 10–100 micrometres in diameter, although definitions vary between texts. Their endothelial lining and thin circumferential smooth-muscle coat permit powerful local control of blood flow.

notes.A: A diameter of one to two millimetres is more consistent with a small or muscular artery than a typical arteriole.
notes.C: Eight micrometres is near the diameter of many capillaries and is smaller than the usual arteriole teaching range.
notes.D: The range of 0.1–1 millimetre is commonly assigned to small arteries possessing more medial muscle layers than typical arterioles.
notes.E: Vessels exceeding ten millimetres are large conducting vessels, not the small resistance vessels that feed capillary networks.

questions.stem: The tunica media of a small artery can have as many as:
questions.why: Small arteries possess several concentric smooth-muscle layers, with around eight layers a conventional upper teaching estimate. They lie between larger muscular distributing arteries and arterioles, which generally have fewer medial muscle layers.

notes.A: One or two smooth-muscle layers are more characteristic of typical arterioles than the upper range of small arterial media.
notes.B: Numerous fenestrated elastic lamellae characterise elastic arteries such as the aorta, rather than small arteries with predominantly muscular media.
notes.D: Incomplete smooth-muscle coverage is described in classical metarteriole models, not the usual multilayered media of a small artery.
notes.E: A vessel lacking a continuous smooth-muscle coat may be a capillary or postcapillary venule, rather than a small artery.

questions.stem: In an arteriole, the tunica intima consists of endothelium, basal lamina and:
questions.why: Arteriolar intima consists of endothelium, basal lamina and very little subendothelial connective tissue. Larger arterioles may possess an internal elastic lamina, but smaller examples generally lack a conspicuous elastic boundary.

notes.A: A prominent thick internal elastic lamina is more characteristic of muscular arteries, although larger arterioles may possess a thinner lamina.
notes.B: Arteriolar smooth muscle is mainly circumferential and belongs to the tunica media, rather than the endothelial intima.
notes.C: Multiple fenestrated elastic lamellae constitute the media of elastic arteries, not the scant intimal connective tissue of arterioles.
notes.E: The thin arteriolar wall receives nutrients by diffusion and does not generally contain a subendothelial vasa vasorum network.

questions.stem: The intermediate filaments around the nucleus of capillary endothelial cells are:
questions.why: They have a supportive role.

questions.stem: Capillary endothelial cells are joined mainly by:
questions.why: Capillary endothelial cells communicate through specialised intercellular junctions, including occluding junctions that regulate paracellular permeability. Their continuity and complexity vary between vascular beds, with brain endothelial junctions being particularly restrictive.

notes.B: Adherens junctions support endothelial cohesion, but do not alone account for the occluding junctions regulating capillary paracellular permeability.
notes.C: Hemidesmosomes anchor epithelial cells to underlying basement membrane rather than principally joining adjacent capillary endothelial cells.
notes.D: Gap junctions facilitate intercellular communication but are not the sole junctional structures controlling endothelial cell adhesion and permeability.
notes.E: Intercalated discs connect cardiomyocytes through specialised junctions, rather than forming the usual junctions between capillary endothelial cells.

questions.stem: Continuous capillaries let molecules pass between endothelial cells only if they are smaller than about:
questions.why: Larger molecules cross by pinocytotic vesicles.

questions.stem: Fenestrations in fenestrated capillaries are about:
questions.why: Fenestrated capillaries possess transcellular endothelial pores measuring tens of nanometres, commonly described around 60–100 nm depending on tissue and preparation. These pores facilitate fluid and solute exchange while basal lamina remains present.

notes.A: Eight to ten micrometres approximates the width of an entire small capillary, not a single endothelial fenestration.
notes.B: Four to five nanometres is substantially smaller than the usual endothelial fenestration diameter, closer to molecular dimensions.
notes.D: Ten to twenty nanometres is smaller than the conventional tens-of-nanometres diameter of most endothelial fenestrations in histological descriptions.
notes.E: One to two micrometres exceeds the usual fenestration diameter by more than an order of magnitude and suggests much larger openings.

questions.stem: When the gut is NOT absorbing, its fenestrated capillaries:

options.label: A
options.text: lose their basal lamina almost completely

options.label: D
options.text: have fewer fenestrations and thicker walls

options.label: E
options.text: close their lumens and stop all flow

questions.why: During absorption the wall thins and fenestrations increase.

questions.stem: Endothelial cells that are spindle-shaped with gaps between them are typical of the sinusoids of the:
questions.why: Splenic venous sinuses are lined by elongated stave cells arranged longitudinally with narrow intercellular slits. Erythrocytes must deform through these openings when returning from red pulp cords to the venous circulation.

notes.A: Hepatic sinusoids have fenestrated discontinuous endothelial cells and Kupffer macrophages, rather than the characteristic splenic longitudinal stave-cell arrangement.
notes.B: Bone marrow sinusoids permit mature blood cells to enter circulation, but the classic stave-cell lining identifies splenic venous sinuses.
notes.C: Renal glomerular capillaries have fenestrated endothelium and a specialised basement membrane, not the splenic sinusoidal stave-cell arrangement.
notes.D: Brain capillaries have restrictive continuous endothelium with tight junctions, rather than slit-containing sinusoidal walls.

questions.stem: Arteriovenous shunts are common in the:

options.label: A
options.text: skin of the fingertips, nose and lips

options.label: B
options.text: alveolar walls of the lungs and pleura

questions.why: Cutaneous arteriovenous anastomoses provide direct routes between arterial and venous vessels, bypassing nutritive capillary beds. They are prominent in specialised skin regions and regulate heat transfer by adjusting blood flow near the body surface.

notes.B: Pulmonary alveolar walls contain dense gas-exchange capillary networks, rather than being classic sites of cutaneous thermoregulatory arteriovenous anastomoses.
notes.C: Renal glomeruli consist of capillary networks between afferent and efferent arterioles, supporting filtration rather than cutaneous heat exchange.
notes.D: Ventricular myocardium contains coronary capillaries supporting oxygen delivery, rather than the characteristic surface thermoregulatory shunts.
notes.E: Hepatic sinusoids receive portal and arterial blood for exchange with hepatocytes, not specialised cutaneous arteriovenous heat-regulating pathways.

questions.stem: Veins are classified into four types according to their:
questions.why: Veins are conventionally classified by calibre into venules, small veins, medium veins and large veins. Their wall organisation changes with size, although exact diameter boundaries and terminology differ between histology references.

notes.A: Valve number varies with location and haemodynamic demands, rather than defining the standard four calibre-based venous categories.
notes.C: Smooth-muscle orientation helps identify certain large veins, but the conventional broad classification is primarily based on vessel size.
notes.D: Elastic content varies with venous wall structure and location, rather than providing the principal criterion for the four categories.
notes.E: Anatomical location influences venous architecture and valve distribution, but calibre is the usual basis of this histological classification.

questions.stem: Small veins measure:
questions.why: Small veins are conventionally described as vessels below approximately one millimetre in diameter, between venules and medium veins. Their wall has developing smooth-muscle and connective-tissue layers supporting venous drainage from microvascular beds.

notes.A: A diameter extending to ten millimetres includes many medium veins, rather than defining the narrower category of small veins.
notes.B: Diameters exceeding ten millimetres are conventionally assigned to large veins, rather than small collecting veins downstream of venules.
notes.D: Eight to ten micrometres approximates the calibre of many capillaries, which lack the organised muscular wall of small veins.
notes.E: Small veins have a range of diameters rather than one exact universal calibre of 0.1 millimetre.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a medium vein?
questions.why: Also the radial and tibial veins.

questions.stem: Valves in medium veins are most numerous in the:
questions.why: Venous valves are especially prominent in limb veins, particularly the lower limbs where gravity increases hydrostatic pressure during upright posture. They limit retrograde flow and cooperate with skeletal-muscle contraction to promote venous return.

notes.A: Upper limb veins also possess valves, but lower limb veins have especially important valve networks opposing dependent hydrostatic loading.
notes.B: Many neck veins have fewer valves than limb veins and do not experience the same prolonged dependent hydrostatic loading.
notes.C: Large thoracic central veins are often relatively valveless, rather than containing the most numerous medium-vein valves.
notes.D: Many abdominal veins lack extensive valves, particularly the portal circulation, whereas lower limb venous valves are especially prominent.

questions.stem: The intima of a medium vein may contain:
questions.why: A medium vein may possess a thin, poorly defined internal elastic membrane beneath its endothelial and subendothelial intima. Its media is relatively thin compared with that of an accompanying muscular artery.

notes.B: Multiple concentric fenestrated elastic membranes are characteristic of elastic arterial media rather than the thin intima of medium veins.
notes.C: Cardiac muscle is confined principally to the heart and selected proximal venous extensions, not ordinary medium-vein intima.
notes.D: A thick external elastic lamina is more characteristic of certain muscular arteries, rather than a defining structure within venous intima.
notes.E: Vasa vasorum and vascular nerves are principally associated with outer wall layers, not the ordinary thin luminal intima.

questions.stem: In large veins it is hard to tell where smooth muscle belongs because:

options.label: B
options.text: there is no clear intima–media boundary

options.label: D
options.text: the intima has a thick elastic lamina

questions.why: In large veins the intima is thin and the media poorly developed, so there is no sharp intima-media boundary and the smooth muscle is hard to assign to one layer.

questions.stem: The coronary arteries arise from the:
questions.why: The right and left coronary arteries originate from aortic sinuses immediately above the aortic valve in the proximal ascending aorta. Their branches distribute oxygenated blood to the myocardium and other cardiac tissues.

notes.A: The aortic arch gives rise to major head, neck and upper-limb arterial branches rather than the normal coronary artery origins.
notes.B: The pulmonary trunk carries right ventricular output towards the lungs, and is not the normal source of coronary arterial blood.
notes.D: The descending thoracic aorta supplies thoracic structures through branches, rather than giving rise to the normal coronary ostia.
notes.E: The brachiocephalic trunk supplies the right head, neck and upper limb through its branches, not the normal coronary circulation.

questions.stem: Metarterioles have a diameter of about:
questions.why: Arterioles are 10–100 µm; metarterioles are narrower, about 8 µm.

questions.stem: The smooth muscle around a metarteriole is arranged as:
questions.why: Classical descriptions of metarterioles identify discontinuous smooth-muscle coverage along channels linking arterioles with capillary or thoroughfare pathways. This arrangement differs from the continuous circumferential muscle layers typical of ordinary arterioles.

notes.A: Two complete circumferential smooth-muscle layers are more characteristic of arterioles than the interrupted coverage in the classical metarteriole model.
notes.B: Eight complete muscle layers suggest a small artery, rather than the discontinuously muscular microvascular channel described as a metarteriole.
notes.C: A prominent longitudinal outer muscle coat is characteristic of certain large veins, rather than the classical arrangement of metarteriolar muscle.
notes.D: Fenestrated elastic lamellae are characteristic of elastic arterial media and do not form the principal muscular covering of metarterioles.

questions.stem: A precapillary sphincter is best described as:

options.label: A
options.text: a single smooth muscle cell at a capillary origin

options.label: B
options.text: a valve of intima within a postcapillary venule

options.label: C
options.text: a ring of pericytes around a true capillary

options.label: D
options.text: a thickening of the internal elastic lamina

options.label: E
options.text: a fold of endothelium in the metarteriole

questions.why: In classical microcirculatory diagrams, a precapillary sphincter consists of contractile smooth muscle at a capillary entrance. Its contraction can restrict local capillary perfusion, although such discrete structures are not universal across tissues.

notes.B: Intimal valves limit retrograde flow in veins or collecting lymphatics, rather than controlling arterial entry into individual capillary branches.
notes.C: Pericytes surround capillaries and regulate aspects of microvascular function, but are not identical to the classical discrete smooth-muscle sphincter.
notes.D: An internal elastic lamina provides mechanical arterial support rather than actively contracting to regulate the entrance of a capillary.
notes.E: Endothelial folds are not the usual contractile mechanism of a precapillary sphincter in classical microvascular descriptions.

questions.stem: A typical capillary is about:

options.label: A
options.text: 80–100 µm wide and under 1 cm long

options.label: B
options.text: 8–10 µm wide and under 1 mm long

options.label: C
options.text: 1–2 µm wide and under 1 mm long

options.label: D
options.text: 8–10 µm wide and over 1 cm long

options.label: E
options.text: 20–30 µm wide and about 5 mm long

questions.why: Typical capillaries are approximately erythrocyte-sized in diameter, often around 5–10 micrometres, and their individual segments are generally short. Their narrow lumina and thin walls bring blood close to surrounding cells for efficient exchange.

notes.A: A width of 80–100 micrometres is substantially larger than a typical capillary and more consistent with larger microvessels.
notes.C: A lumen only one to two micrometres wide would be substantially narrower than most ordinary erythrocyte-transmitting capillary segments.
notes.D: Capillary networks extend through tissues, but individual capillary segments are not generally more than one centimetre long.
notes.E: Widths of 20–30 micrometres may occur in specialised sinusoids or larger microvascular channels rather than ordinary narrow capillaries.

questions.stem: The wall of a capillary consists of:

options.label: A
options.text: endothelium, elastic lamina and smooth muscle

options.label: B
options.text: endothelium, smooth muscle and thin adventitia

options.label: C
options.text: endothelium, basal lamina and occasional pericytes

options.label: D
options.text: mesothelium, basal lamina and a few fibroblasts

options.label: E
options.text: endothelium, collagen layer and vasa vasorum

questions.why: The capillary wall consists primarily of a single endothelial layer and associated basal lamina, with variable pericyte coverage. This thin architecture minimises diffusion distance and permits selective exchange between blood and interstitial fluid.

notes.A: Capillaries lack the distinct elastic lamina and continuous smooth-muscle media characteristic of larger arterial blood vessels.
notes.B: A separate muscular media and adventitia are absent from typical capillary walls, which consist chiefly of endothelial and basal lamina structures.
notes.D: Mesothelium lines serous body cavities; capillaries are lined by vascular endothelium rather than mesothelial cells.
notes.E: Capillary walls are sufficiently thin for diffusion and do not contain the vasa vasorum needed to nourish large vessel walls.

questions.stem: Which organelle feature is described as characteristic of capillary endothelial cells?
questions.why: Many capillary endothelial cells contain numerous caveolae and pinocytotic vesicles participating in transcellular transport. Their abundance varies considerably, with blood–brain barrier endothelium showing particularly low nonspecific vesicular transport.

notes.A: Zymogen granules store digestive enzyme precursors in secretory cells such as pancreatic acinar cells, rather than typifying capillary endothelium.
notes.B: Lamellar bodies store pulmonary surfactant in type II pneumocytes, not the characteristic vesicular transport structures of ordinary capillary endothelium.
notes.C: Basal striations reflect mitochondria associated with membrane infoldings in certain transporting epithelia, rather than typical capillary endothelial cytoplasm.
notes.E: Secretory canaliculi are prominent in certain glandular arrangements, such as gastric parietal cells, rather than defining capillary endothelial ultrastructure.

questions.stem: Continuous capillaries are typically found in:
questions.why: Continuous capillaries have uninterrupted endothelial lining and generally continuous basal lamina. They occur widely in muscle, lung and central nervous tissue, with tissue-specific junctional properties determining their permeability and exchange functions.

notes.A: Liver, spleen and bone marrow commonly contain specialised discontinuous or sinusoidal vascular beds rather than predominantly typical continuous capillaries.
notes.B: Renal glomeruli and intestinal mucosa contain fenestrated capillaries suited to rapid filtration or absorption, rather than ordinary continuous capillaries.
notes.C: Endocrine glands and intestinal mucosa commonly possess fenestrated capillaries facilitating rapid hormone or nutrient exchange.
notes.D: Splenic sinuses are specialised discontinuous vessels and renal glomeruli are fenestrated, so this grouping does not identify typical continuous capillary distribution.

questions.stem: Fenestrated capillaries are typically found in:

options.label: B
options.text: skeletal muscle, lung, skin and brain

questions.why: Fenestrated capillaries contain endothelial pores facilitating rapid fluid and solute transfer. They commonly occur in endocrine organs, renal glomeruli and intestinal mucosa, where hormone exchange, filtration or absorption requires relatively high vascular permeability.

notes.B: Skeletal muscle, lung, skin and brain predominantly contain continuous capillaries, although their endothelial permeability differs substantially by tissue.
notes.C: Liver, spleen and bone marrow characteristically contain specialised sinusoidal or discontinuous vascular beds rather than ordinary fenestrated capillaries.
notes.D: Cardiac muscle, skin and peripheral nerve microvessels commonly exhibit continuous endothelium rather than the characteristic fenestrated exchange pattern.
notes.E: Brain, spinal cord and retinal vascular barriers use restrictive continuous endothelium rather than fenestrations permitting relatively unrestricted solute passage.

questions.stem: Seen from the lumen, the diaphragm of a fenestration looks like a cartwheel with a central thickening and:
questions.why: The diaphragm is thin and non-membranous.

questions.stem: Another name for fenestrated capillaries is:
questions.why: Fenestrated capillaries are traditionally termed visceral capillaries because they occur in many secretory and absorptive organs. Endothelial fenestrations facilitate exchange while a generally continuous basal lamina remains beneath the endothelial cells.

notes.A: Somatic capillaries is an older term for continuous capillaries, rather than those with transcellular endothelial fenestrations.
notes.B: Sinusoidal capillaries have larger irregular lumina and often discontinuous basal lamina, differing from conventional fenestrated vascular beds.
notes.D: Discontinuous capillaries exhibit larger structural interruptions and variable basal lamina, rather than being synonymous with ordinary fenestrated capillaries.
notes.E: Thoroughfare channels belong to classical descriptions of microvascular routing and do not define the endothelial fenestrated capillary category.

questions.stem: Compared with other capillaries, sinusoids are:

options.label: A
options.text: smaller and more regular in shape

options.label: B
options.text: longer, with a thicker basal lamina

options.label: D
options.text: larger and more irregular in shape

questions.why: Sinusoidal capillaries generally have larger, irregular lumina compared with ordinary capillaries. Their specialised endothelial arrangements and variably discontinuous basal lamina facilitate exchange of macromolecules or cells in tissues such as liver and bone marrow.

notes.A: Typical sinusoids are wider and less regular than ordinary capillaries, rather than being smaller with a uniform circular profile.
notes.B: Sinusoidal basal lamina is often discontinuous or absent, rather than consistently thicker than that of conventional capillary beds.
notes.C: A narrow lumen and restrictive endothelial junctions are more characteristic of continuous capillaries than specialised sinusoidal vascular channels.
notes.E: Sinusoids lack a continuous muscular media and typically have irregular courses, rather than straight muscular walls.

questions.stem: The basal lamina of a sinusoidal capillary is:

options.label: B
options.text: double, with a middle dense layer

options.label: C
options.text: fused with a layer of smooth muscle

questions.why: Sinusoidal vascular beds commonly possess discontinuous or poorly developed basal lamina, allowing specialised exchange with adjacent tissue. The precise extent varies between organs, with hepatic sinusoids particularly notable for lacking a conventional continuous basement membrane.

notes.A: A thick continuous basal lamina characterises specialised filtration structures such as glomerular capillaries, rather than typical discontinuous hepatic sinusoids.
notes.B: A double dense-layer basement membrane is not a defining feature of sinusoidal vessels, which commonly have interrupted extracellular support.
notes.C: Sinusoids generally lack a continuous smooth-muscle media and do not have basal lamina fused to a muscular coat.
notes.D: An internal elastic lamina is an arterial wall structure and does not replace the discontinuous basal lamina of sinusoidal capillaries.

questions.stem: The main role of arteriovenous shunts at the body surface is:
questions.why: Cutaneous arteriovenous shunts adjust blood flow through superficial vascular pathways, bypassing local nutritive capillary beds when open. Their sympathetic regulation helps control transfer of heat between the body and surrounding environment.

notes.B: Gas exchange occurs chiefly across pulmonary alveolar capillaries, rather than being the principal function of cutaneous arteriovenous anastomoses.
notes.C: Lymph nodes filter lymph before its return to venous circulation, rather than cutaneous arterial-to-venous shunts filtering tissue fluid.
notes.D: Arterial baroreceptors detect vascular stretch to regulate pressure, rather than thermoregulatory shunts serving chiefly as pressure-sensing structures.
notes.E: Nutrient exchange occurs mainly across capillary beds, whereas direct arteriovenous channels can bypass these exchange surfaces.

questions.stem: Compared with arteries, the coats (tunics) of veins are:
questions.why: Venous tunics are generally less sharply demarcated than arterial tunics because elastic laminae are less prominent and smooth muscle blends with connective tissue. The adventitia often constitutes the largest portion of the wall.

notes.A: Arterial elastic boundaries are generally clearer, so veins typically have less distinct rather than more distinct tunics.
notes.C: Veins usually have thinner media and less organised elastic tissue than corresponding arteries, reflecting lower intravascular pressures.
notes.D: Distinct internal and external elastic laminae are more characteristic of muscular arteries than the usual venous wall.
notes.E: Most veins possess identifiable intimal, medial and adventitial components, although their boundaries are less conspicuous than in arteries.

questions.stem: Venules are subclassified as:
questions.why: Venules are conventionally divided into postcapillary and muscular venules. Postcapillary venules have endothelial walls with pericytes, while larger muscular venules acquire continuous smooth-muscle coverage as they approach small veins.

notes.A: Elastic and muscular categories are principally applied to arteries, rather than the usual histological subclassification of venules.
notes.B: Continuous and fenestrated describe endothelial capillary architecture, not the principal classification of venules by muscular wall development.
notes.D: Superficial and deep refer to anatomical location of veins, rather than the conventional wall-based subclassification of venules.
notes.E: Somatic and visceral are traditional capillary terms and do not identify the two conventional types of venule.

questions.stem: Medium veins can have a diameter of up to about:
questions.why: Medium veins are conventionally classified as vessels approximately one to ten millimetres in diameter, though boundaries vary by reference. They typically have a relatively thin media, thicker adventitia and often valves in limb locations.

notes.A: One millimetre approximates the conventional lower boundary of medium veins, rather than their usual upper diameter limit.
notes.B: A tenth of a millimetre is within the calibre of small venous vessels rather than the upper range of medium veins.
notes.C: Twenty-five millimetres is more consistent with a large central vein than the conventional upper diameter of medium veins.
notes.E: Fifty millimetres substantially exceeds the usual medium-vein category and is associated with much larger venous structures.

questions.stem: Compared with a medium-sized artery, the tunica media of a medium vein is:

options.label: B
options.text: equal, with a prominent elastic lamina

options.label: E
options.text: thinner, with collagen between the muscle

questions.why: Medium veins operate under lower pressure than corresponding muscular arteries and possess a relatively thin tunica media. Circumferential smooth-muscle cells are interspersed with collagen and elastic fibres, while the adventitia is relatively prominent.

notes.A: Numerous medial elastic lamellae characterise elastic arteries, rather than the comparatively thin media of medium-sized veins.
notes.B: Medium veins generally have a thinner media and less conspicuous internal elastic lamina than corresponding muscular arteries.
notes.C: Medium veins retain a smooth-muscle-containing tunica media even though their adventitia is often comparatively thicker and more conspicuous.
notes.D: Prominent longitudinal smooth muscle is particularly characteristic of the adventitia of large veins rather than the medium-vein media.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a large vein?
questions.why: The hepatic portal vein is a large vessel conveying nutrient-rich blood from gastrointestinal organs and spleen towards hepatic sinusoids. In conventional histological size classifications it is grouped with large veins rather than smaller peripheral veins.

notes.B: The popliteal vein is commonly grouped with medium peripheral veins, although its actual diameter varies with physiological conditions.
notes.C: Radial veins accompany the radial artery and are smaller peripheral vessels rather than the major hepatic portal collecting vein.
notes.D: Tibial veins are peripheral deep veins of smaller calibre than the principal trunk conveying blood to the liver.
notes.E: The great saphenous vein is a long superficial limb vein generally classed as medium calibre despite its extensive length.

questions.stem: The tunica media of a large vein contains circumferential smooth muscle, collagen fibres and:
questions.why: The media of a large vein contains circumferential smooth muscle interspersed with collagen, elastic fibres and connective-tissue cells including fibroblasts. This comparatively thin layer contrasts with the substantial longitudinal muscle of the adventitia.

notes.A: Elastic cartilage is a specialised supporting tissue and is not a normal component of the smooth-muscle media of veins.
notes.C: Repeated fenestrated elastic lamellae are characteristic of elastic arteries rather than the relatively thin media of large veins.
notes.D: Purkinje fibres are specialised cardiac conducting cells and do not form part of the normal venous tunica media.
notes.E: Vasa vasorum may nourish outer vessel walls, but the venous media contains smooth muscle and extracellular matrix rather than vessels alone.

questions.stem: The great saphenous vein drains into the:
questions.why: The great saphenous vein ascends medially through the lower limb and pierces the deep fascia at the saphenous opening. It joins the femoral vein at the saphenofemoral junction, returning superficial venous blood to deep circulation.

notes.A: The small saphenous vein commonly drains into the popliteal vein, whereas the great saphenous vein joins the femoral vein.
notes.B: The femoral vein continues proximally as the external iliac vein, but the great saphenous vein normally joins it before that transition.
notes.D: The small saphenous vein drains the posterior lower leg and does not normally receive the terminal great saphenous vein.
notes.E: The internal iliac vein drains much of the pelvis and is not the usual direct termination of the great saphenous vein.

questions.stem: In the great saphenous vein, longitudinal smooth muscle bundles are found in the:
questions.why: The media has a thick circular muscle coat.

questions.stem: The walls of coronary arteries are thicker than those of comparable limb arteries because of:

options.label: A
options.text: many more elastic lamellae in the media

options.label: E
options.text: more circular smooth muscle in the media

questions.why: They are classed as medium-sized muscular arteries.

questions.stem: The largest lymphatic vessel, which empties into veins on the left side, is the:
questions.why: The thoracic duct is the largest lymphatic collecting vessel, draining most of the body except the right upper quadrant. It usually empties near the junction of the left internal jugular and subclavian veins.

notes.B: The right lymphatic duct or separate right lymphatic trunks drain the right upper quadrant rather than most of the body.
notes.C: The cisterna chyli is a variable dilated origin of the thoracic duct, not the terminal vessel entering left-sided veins.
notes.D: The left jugular trunk drains lymph from the left head and neck, rather than collecting lymph from most body regions.
notes.E: The intestinal trunk carries lymph from abdominal digestive organs towards the thoracic duct, rather than being the largest terminal collecting vessel.

questions.stem: Before lymph is returned to the blood, it passes through:
questions.why: Lymph normally passes through lymph nodes along collecting pathways before returning to the venous circulation. Nodal sinuses expose lymph-borne antigens and particles to macrophages and lymphocytes, supporting filtration and adaptive immune surveillance.

notes.A: The spleen filters circulating blood rather than functioning as the principal filter of lymph in collecting lymphatic vessels.
notes.C: The thymus supports T-cell maturation and lacks the afferent lymphatic filtration arrangement characteristic of lymph nodes.
notes.D: The liver processes portal blood and performs numerous metabolic functions, rather than being the conventional lymph-filtering organ along collecting pathways.
notes.E: Bone marrow produces blood cells and supports lymphocyte development but does not replace lymph nodes in filtration of lymph.

questions.stem: Lymphatic vessels carry lymph:

options.label: C
options.text: in one direction, aided by valves

options.label: D
options.text: only when the heart is in systole

questions.why: Collecting lymphatic vessels contain valves and contractile smooth muscle that support unidirectional movement towards venous drainage sites. External muscle activity and pressure changes also assist lymph propulsion, while valves limit retrograde flow.

notes.A: Valves in collecting lymphatics prevent substantial backward flow, rather than allowing unrestricted movement in both directions.
notes.B: Initial lymphatics collect interstitial fluid from tissues and convey it towards venous circulation, not away from veins into tissues.
notes.D: Lymph propulsion involves intrinsic and extrinsic pumping mechanisms and is not limited to periods of cardiac systole.
notes.E: Unidirectional movement is supported by valves in collecting lymphatic vessels, rather than occurring through entirely valveless collecting channels.

questions.stem: Elastic arteries have an outer diameter of more than about:
questions.why: Muscular arteries are 10–1 mm; small arteries 1–0.1 mm.

questions.stem: The main role of small arteries (1–0.1 mm) is to:

options.label: A
options.text: conduct blood from the heart by elastic recoil

options.label: C
options.text: drain capillary beds into the veins

options.label: D
options.text: return blood to the heart at low pressure

options.label: E
options.text: distribute blood to arterioles, adjusting flow

questions.why: Small arteries distribute blood into arteriolar resistance networks and regulate regional perfusion through contraction of their circumferential smooth muscle. Their muscular architecture is suited to adjusting calibre rather than storing large amounts of elastic energy.

notes.A: Elastic conducting arteries buffer pulsatile ventricular output through expansion and recoil, unlike the predominant muscular organisation of small arteries.
notes.B: Capillaries provide the principal thin-walled exchange surfaces for metabolites, rather than small arteries with several smooth-muscle layers.
notes.C: Venules collect blood from capillary beds and convey it towards veins, rather than supplying arterial inflow to microcirculation.
notes.D: Veins return blood towards the heart at relatively low pressure, whereas small arteries distribute arterial blood towards arterioles.

questions.stem: According to the comparison table, the media of a large vein has:

options.label: A
options.text: more than 5 layers of muscle, with much collagen

options.label: B
options.text: 1–3 layers of muscle with no collagen

options.label: C
options.text: many elastic lamellae alternating with muscle

options.label: D
options.text: scattered muscle cells and pericytes only

options.label: E
options.text: 3–10 layers of muscle and no collagen

questions.why: Small veins have 2–3 loose layers; medium veins 3–5.

questions.stem: The semilunar valves of the aorta and pulmonary trunk each have:
questions.why: The aortic and pulmonary valves normally each possess three pocket-shaped semilunar cusps. Reversal of the pressure gradient after ventricular ejection fills these cusps and brings their free edges together, preventing arterial backflow.

notes.A: Two leaflets characterise the mitral valve, although a bicuspid aortic valve can occur as a congenital anatomical variant.
notes.C: Four semilunar cusps represent an uncommon anatomical variant rather than the normal arrangement of either semilunar valve.
notes.D: A single cusp is not the normal semilunar configuration needed to form the three-part closure of these arterial valves.
notes.E: Five cusps are not the usual anatomical arrangement of the aortic or pulmonary semilunar valve in healthy hearts.

questions.stem: The atrioventricular valves prevent blood flowing back from the:

options.label: D
options.text: pulmonary trunk into the right ventricle

options.label: E
options.text: left atrium into the right atrium

questions.why: Atrioventricular valves close when ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure during systole, preventing regurgitation into the atria. Chordae tendineae and papillary muscles prevent excessive leaflet prolapse while the pressure gradient maintains valve closure.

notes.A: Atrioventricular valves lie between atria and ventricles, not at the entrances of the great veins into the atria.
notes.B: The aortic semilunar valve prevents reverse flow from the aorta into the left ventricle, rather than the mitral valve.
notes.D: The pulmonary semilunar valve prevents regurgitation from the pulmonary trunk into the right ventricle during ventricular relaxation.
notes.E: The interatrial septum normally separates the atria; atrioventricular valves do not directly regulate flow between right and left atria.

questions.stem: In elastic arteries, vasa vasorum and nerves lie in the:
questions.why: Vasa vasorum enter thick elastic arterial walls through the adventitia and supply the outer media, where diffusion from luminal blood is insufficient. Vascular nerves are also concentrated in the adventitia and influence underlying smooth muscle.

notes.A: The innermost intima normally receives nutrients chiefly by diffusion from luminal blood, rather than containing the principal vasa vasorum network.
notes.B: Although the adventitia contains vasa vasorum and nerves, the network can extend into outer media rather than primarily into intima.
notes.C: The endothelial monolayer is nourished directly by luminal blood and does not contain separate vessels or autonomic nerve bundles.
notes.E: Vasa vasorum and vascular nerves are especially associated with adventitia, not exclusively restricted to the smooth-muscle and elastic media.

questions.stem: The internal elastic membrane of an elastic artery is:
questions.why: The internal elastic lamina of an elastic artery is difficult to distinguish because numerous similar elastic lamellae occupy the adjacent media. In muscular arteries, the internal elastic lamina contrasts more distinctly with surrounding smooth muscle.

notes.A: A sharply prominent internal elastic lamina is particularly characteristic of muscular arteries, where adjacent medial smooth muscle makes it conspicuous.
notes.B: An elastic arterial intimal boundary can be present but poorly distinguishable, rather than necessarily being absent in every elastic artery.
notes.C: A duplicated elastic boundary is not the characteristic identifying feature; the repeated medial elastic lamellae obscure the internal lamina.
notes.D: Calcification can occur with ageing or vascular disease, but is not the normal defining histological appearance of the internal elastic lamina.

questions.stem: Blood that passes through two capillary beds in series before returning to the heart is flowing through a:
questions.why: A portal system connects two capillary networks in series through an intervening vessel before blood returns to the heart. The hepatic portal system links gastrointestinal capillaries to hepatic sinusoids, allowing absorbed substances to reach the liver directly.

notes.B: A thoroughfare channel bypasses some capillary exchange pathways rather than linking two distinct capillary beds in series.
notes.C: An arteriovenous shunt directly connects arterial and venous vessels, bypassing rather than sequentially perfusing two exchange networks.
notes.D: Collateral circulation provides alternative routes around an obstructed or restricted pathway rather than defining sequential passage through two capillary beds.
notes.E: An end artery lacks substantial effective collateral supply to its territory, rather than describing a vessel connecting two capillary networks.

questions.stem: The epicardium is covered on its outer surface by:
questions.why: The epicardium is the visceral layer of serous pericardium, covered externally by simple squamous mesothelium. Beneath it lies connective tissue containing variable adipose tissue, coronary vessels and nerves supplying the cardiac wall.

notes.A: Endothelium lines cardiovascular lumina, whereas mesothelium covers the heart's external serous surface facing the pericardial cavity.
notes.C: Stratified squamous epithelium protects surfaces subject to abrasion, rather than forming the thin lubricated serosal covering of the heart.
notes.D: The normal epicardial surface is lined by flattened mesothelial cells rather than a conventional simple cuboidal secretory epithelium.
