notes.E: Transitional epithelium lines distensible urinary passages and is not the epithelial covering of the visceral serous pericardium.

questions.stem: About the zones of the airway:

options.label: A
options.text: The conducting zone warms, moistens and filters inspired air

options.label: B
options.text: The trachea is generation 0 and the main bronchi generation 1

options.label: C
options.text: Terminal bronchioles belong to the respiratory zone

notes.A: Conducting passages warm and humidify air while mucus, cilia and other defences remove inhaled material.
notes.B: The classical airway model numbers the trachea zero and its first major bronchial branches one.
notes.C: Terminal bronchioles are the final purely conducting airways, with no alveoli opening into their walls.
notes.D: Respiratory bronchioles approximately occupy generations seventeen through nineteen in the classical symmetrical branching model.
notes.E: Alveolar sacs are conventionally placed near generation twenty-three in the idealised Weibel airway model.

questions.why: The conducting zone conditions and transports air through terminal bronchioles; the respiratory zone begins where alveoli interrupt bronchiolar walls. In the classical Weibel model, airway generations provide approximate numerical landmarks rather than invariant anatomy.

questions.stem: Which function is NOT listed for the respiratory system?
questions.why: The respiratory system exchanges gases, regulates carbon dioxide-dependent pH, supports phonation and olfaction, and participates in vascular metabolism through ACE. Erythropoietin is produced predominantly by renal interstitial cells responding to hypoxia.

notes.B: Ventilation regulates arterial carbon dioxide tension and thereby contributes rapidly to control of extracellular hydrogen ion concentration.
notes.C: Pulmonary vascular endothelium expresses abundant angiotensin-converting enzyme, participating in angiotensin II formation and bradykinin metabolism.
notes.D: Airflow carries volatile odorants towards specialised nasal olfactory epithelium, supporting the detection of smell.
notes.E: Air passing through the larynx vibrates vocal folds during phonation, supporting production of sound and speech.

questions.stem: In the conducting airways:

options.label: E
options.text: the epithelium rests on a thin basement membrane in the trachea

notes.A: Smooth muscle runs concentrically (spirally) around the airway.
notes.C: The lamina propria contains bronchus-associated lymphoid tissue (BALT).
notes.D: Seromucous glands lie in the submucosa.
notes.E: The tracheal basement membrane is notably thick.

questions.why: Conducting airways have respiratory epithelium on a basement membrane (thick in the trachea), a lamina propria with BALT and a submucosa with seromucous glands.

questions.stem: Cells of the respiratory epithelium:

options.label: A
options.text: Goblet cells secrete mucus that traps particles and absorbs water-soluble gases

options.label: B
options.text: Ciliated cells move mucus toward the pharynx

options.label: C
options.text: Brush cells are chemosensory, with afferent nerve endings at their base

options.label: D
options.text: Small granule (K) cells are the stem cells of the epithelium

options.label: E
options.text: Small granule cells contain serotonin, calcitonin and bombesin

notes.A: Goblet cells secrete mucins that form mucus, trapping inhaled particles and dissolving selected gaseous substances.
notes.B: Ciliated epithelial cells beat in coordinated directions, transporting airway mucus towards the pharynx for clearance.
notes.C: Brush cells possess apical microvilli and participate in chemosensory signalling, sometimes through associated afferent nerve fibres.
notes.D: Basal cells serve as major epithelial progenitors; small granule cells are specialised pulmonary neuroendocrine cells.
notes.E: Pulmonary neuroendocrine cells can contain serotonin and peptides including calcitonin-related products and bombesin-like substances.

questions.why: Respiratory epithelium contains specialised cells for mucociliary clearance, sensory signalling and epithelial renewal. Basal cells supply progenitors, while pulmonary neuroendocrine small granule cells contain locally active peptides and amines.

questions.stem: Cigarette smoking changes the respiratory mucosa mainly by:

options.label: A
options.text: loss of all goblet cells in the airway

options.label: B
options.text: increasing goblet cell number and size

options.label: E
options.text: replacing basal cells with brush cells

questions.why: Chronic cigarette smoke exposure irritates airway epithelium and promotes goblet-cell hyperplasia, hypertrophy and mucus hypersecretion. Associated ciliary dysfunction and epithelial remodelling impair mucociliary clearance and increase susceptibility to persistent airway obstruction.

notes.A: Chronic smoke exposure commonly increases mucus-secreting cell populations rather than eliminating all goblet cells from conducting airways.
notes.C: Ciliary injury and loss can accompany smoking, but motile cilia do not simply transform into ordinary absorptive microvilli.
notes.D: Airway cartilage may undergo age-related or pathological changes, but goblet-cell expansion is a characteristic epithelial response to smoke.
notes.E: Basal progenitors participate in epithelial repair and remodelling, rather than being systematically replaced by brush cells during chronic smoking.

questions.stem: Bowman's glands of the olfactory mucosa function mainly to:

options.label: A
options.text: secrete mucus that traps dust particles

options.label: C
options.text: dissolve odorants and wash them away

options.label: E
options.text: warm the inspired air by heat exchange

questions.why: Bowman's glands in olfactory lamina propria secrete a watery fluid onto the sensory epithelium. This fluid helps dissolve odorants for receptor interaction and washes away previously bound molecules, allowing detection of new stimuli.

notes.A: Respiratory goblet cells and seromucous glands produce particle-trapping mucus, whereas olfactory glands chiefly provide watery secretion for odorant processing.
notes.B: Olfactory secretions may contain binding proteins, but pigment production is not the principal mechanism clearing and dissolving odorants.
notes.D: Basal progenitor cells replace olfactory sensory neurons, rather than Bowman's glands directly generating new receptor cells.
notes.E: Rich nasal vascular networks contribute to warming inspired air; Bowman's glands chiefly maintain the olfactory epithelial fluid environment.

questions.stem: Bronchi are best identified histologically by:

options.label: A
options.text: C-shaped cartilage rings and trachealis muscle

options.label: B
options.text: club cells and the absence of glands

options.label: D
options.text: cartilage plates and circular smooth muscle

questions.why: Intrapulmonary bronchi have irregular hyaline cartilage plates, a circumferential or spiral smooth-muscle layer and respiratory epithelium with submucosal glands. Cartilage and glands distinguish them from bronchioles, which lack these structures.

notes.A: C-shaped cartilage rings and a posterior trachealis muscle identify the trachea or extrapulmonary large bronchial pattern rather than intrapulmonary bronchi.
notes.B: Club cells become prominent in bronchioles, which lack submucosal glands and cartilaginous support unlike intrapulmonary bronchi.
notes.C: Cuboidal epithelium interrupted by alveolar openings identifies respiratory bronchioles rather than cartilage-supported intrapulmonary bronchi.
notes.E: Bronchial cartilage is hyaline rather than elastic, although seromucous submucosal glands are indeed present in bronchi.

questions.stem: Respiratory bronchioles differ from terminal bronchioles mainly by:
questions.why: Respiratory bronchioles represent the transition from conducting airways to gas-exchange passages because alveoli interrupt their walls. Terminal bronchioles retain an uninterrupted bronchiolar epithelial lining and lack alveolar openings along their course.

notes.A: Both terminal and respiratory bronchioles lack cartilage, so cartilaginous plates cannot distinguish these two small airway segments.
notes.B: Goblet cells are sparse or absent in normal distal bronchioles, rather than providing the defining respiratory bronchiole characteristic.
notes.C: Both types of bronchiole lack submucosal seromucous glands, which occur in larger conducting airways such as bronchi.
notes.D: Bronchiolar epithelia are generally simple cuboidal distally; alveolar openings rather than epithelial stratification identify respiratory bronchioles.

questions.stem: Type I pneumocytes:

options.label: B
options.text: make up about 40% of alveolar cells

options.label: C
options.text: cover about 95% of the alveolar surface

options.label: E
options.text: can divide to replace lost alveolar cells

notes.A: Type I cells are very thin squamous cells.
notes.B: They make up about 40% of alveolar lining cells.
notes.C: They cover about 95% of the alveolar surface.
notes.D: Surfactant comes from type II cells.
notes.E: Type I cells cannot divide; type II cells replace them.

questions.why: Type I pneumocytes are thin squamous cells covering most of the alveolar surface for gas exchange; type II cells make surfactant and replace them.

questions.stem: Which is NOT part of the blood–air barrier?
questions.why: The thin gas-exchange barrier comprises alveolar lining fluid and surfactant, type I pneumocyte cytoplasm, closely apposed or fused basal laminae and capillary endothelium. Type II pneumocytes principally secrete surfactant.

notes.B: Type I pneumocytes provide an extremely thin epithelial component across which respiratory gases diffuse between alveolar air and blood.
notes.C: Fused epithelial and endothelial basal laminae minimise diffusion distance at the thin portions of the interalveolar septum.
notes.D: Capillary endothelial cells form the vascular cellular component of the diffusion barrier and directly contact circulating blood.
notes.E: The surfactant-containing lining fluid lies at the air–epithelium interface and is included in physiological descriptions of the diffusion pathway.

questions.stem: In emphysema, the alveolar walls are destroyed mainly by:

options.label: C
options.text: collapse of the pores of Kohn

questions.why: Emphysema involves permanent enlargement of distal airspaces with destruction of alveolar walls. Protease–antiprotease imbalance, oxidant injury and inflammation, including neutrophil elastase and macrophage proteases, contribute to loss of elastic support.

notes.A: Surfactant lowers alveolar surface tension and its overproduction is not the characteristic mechanism destroying alveolar septal tissue.
notes.C: Pores of Kohn provide collateral alveolar communication rather than their collapse being the principal cause of septal destruction.
notes.D: Type I pneumocytes cover alveolar surfaces; their hyperplasia is not the principal proteolytic mechanism of emphysematous wall loss.
notes.E: Bronchial cartilage fibrosis alters airway mechanics but does not account for destruction of the distal alveolar septa characteristic of emphysema.

questions.stem: An immotile-cilia syndrome affecting the airways is:
questions.why: Kartagener syndrome is a form of primary ciliary dyskinesia associated with chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis and situs inversus. Abnormal motile ciliary function impairs mucociliary clearance, predisposing the airways to recurrent infection.

notes.A: Cystic fibrosis involves abnormal CFTR-mediated ion transport and viscous secretions, rather than the primary motile ciliary defect described.
notes.B: Hyaline membrane disease results principally from neonatal surfactant deficiency, rather than inherited impairment of respiratory ciliary motility.
notes.D: Atelectasis describes loss of aeration or collapse of lung tissue and is not the specific inherited ciliary syndrome.
notes.E: Sleep apnoea involves recurrent interruption of breathing during sleep, rather than primary impairment of mucociliary transport.

questions.stem: The respiratory zone of the airway begins at the:
questions.why: Respiratory bronchioles mark the beginning of the respiratory zone because alveoli interrupt their bronchiolar walls. Gas exchange becomes possible at these openings and continues through alveolar ducts and sacs.

notes.A: Terminal bronchioles are the last purely conducting airways and do not have alveoli interrupting their walls.
notes.B: Alveolar ducts are downstream respiratory passages, rather than the first airway generation where alveolar gas exchange becomes possible.
notes.C: Tertiary bronchi possess cartilage and glands and belong to the conducting zone before bronchiolar and alveolar regions.
notes.E: Alveolar sacs are distal clusters of alveoli, encountered after respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts in the branching airway.

questions.stem: The epithelium lining most of the conducting airways is:

options.label: C
options.text: simple squamous with type I cells

questions.why: Most larger conducting airways are lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells. Mucus traps inhaled particles and coordinated ciliary movement carries the mucus towards the pharynx.

notes.A: Nonkeratinised stratified squamous epithelium protects selected abrasion-prone regions such as true vocal folds, not most conducting airways.
notes.B: Simple cuboidal epithelium with club cells characterises distal bronchioles, rather than the predominant lining of larger conducting passages.
notes.C: Simple squamous type I pneumocytes line alveolar gas-exchange surfaces, not the main conducting airway epithelium.
notes.D: Stratified columnar epithelium is uncommon in respiratory passages; apparent layering in typical respiratory epithelium reflects pseudostratification.

questions.stem: The stem cells of the respiratory epithelium are the:
questions.why: Basal cells attach to the basement membrane beneath the taller respiratory epithelial cells. They act as progenitors capable of generating ciliated and secretory epithelial populations during homeostasis and repair.

notes.B: Brush cells participate in chemosensory signalling rather than constituting the major progenitor population of pseudostratified respiratory epithelium.
notes.C: Goblet cells are differentiated mucus-secreting cells, whereas basal cells primarily provide epithelial renewal in larger airways.
notes.D: Small granule cells are pulmonary neuroendocrine cells, not the principal multipotent epithelial progenitors of larger conducting airways.
notes.E: Ciliated cells are differentiated cells specialised for mucus transport, rather than the main source of epithelial replacement.

questions.stem: Cells of the respiratory epithelium containing serotonin, calcitonin and bombesin are:
questions.why: Small granule cells are pulmonary neuroendocrine cells containing dense-core secretory vesicles. They release amines and peptides, including serotonin and bombesin-related products, influencing local airway physiology and development.

notes.A: Brush cells have apical microvilli and sensory functions, rather than being the characteristic dense-core pulmonary neuroendocrine population.
notes.C: Club cells secrete protective proteins and metabolise xenobiotics, rather than being primarily identified by serotonin-containing neuroendocrine granules.
notes.D: Basal cells support epithelial renewal, not the secretion of the characteristic amines and peptides stored in neuroendocrine cells.
notes.E: Goblet cells produce mucins for airway surface mucus, rather than the neuroendocrine mediators listed in the stem.

questions.stem: Brush cells of the respiratory epithelium are thought to be:
questions.why: Brush cells possess prominent apical microvilli and express chemosensory signalling components. They can detect luminal substances and communicate with sensory nerves or neighbouring cells, contributing to airway defence responses.

notes.A: Basal cells are the principal stem or progenitor population in larger pseudostratified airways, rather than specialised brush cells.
notes.B: Type II pneumocytes produce most pulmonary alveolar surfactant; brush cells are principally associated with chemosensory epithelial functions.
notes.D: Goblet cells and submucosal glands produce mucus, whereas brush cells are distinguished by sensory-related apical microvilli.
notes.E: Macrophages are phagocytic immune cells rather than specialised epithelial brush cells with chemosensory signalling machinery.

questions.stem: The olfactory receptor cells are:

options.label: C
options.text: multipolar neurons in the lamina propria

questions.why: Olfactory sensory neurons are bipolar neurons with apical dendritic knobs bearing non-motile sensory cilia. Odorant receptors on these cilia initiate signals transmitted along basal axons towards the olfactory bulb.

notes.A: Olfactory receptor neurons are bipolar, and their sensory cilia are non-motile rather than mucus-propelling motile cilia.
notes.B: Olfactory neurons possess specialised sensory cilia, rather than being merely non-neuronal epithelial cells with ordinary microvilli.
notes.C: Olfactory receptor cell bodies lie within the neuroepithelium and are bipolar rather than multipolar lamina propria neurons.
notes.E: Sustentacular cells provide metabolic and structural support; odorant receptor neurons are the principal cells detecting odours.

questions.stem: Reinke oedema develops easily because the superficial lamina propria of the true vocal fold:

options.label: B
options.text: is lined by ciliated respiratory epithelium

options.label: D
options.text: has a thick elastic cartilage plate

options.label: E
options.text: lacks lymphatics and is poorly vascular

questions.why: Fluid that collects in Reinke's space cannot drain away.

notes.A: Glands are in the false folds.

questions.stem: The epithelium of the true vocal fold is:
questions.why: True vocal folds are covered predominantly by nonkeratinised stratified squamous epithelium, especially along their vibrating free surfaces. Multiple cell layers resist mechanical stress from repeated vibration and contact during phonation.

notes.B: Pseudostratified ciliated epithelium lines much of the larynx, but the vibrating true vocal fold requires abrasion-resistant squamous epithelium.
notes.C: Normal true vocal fold squamous epithelium is generally nonkeratinised, rather than possessing the thick keratin layer characteristic of epidermis.
notes.D: Simple columnar goblet-cell epithelium would provide secretion but lacks the multilayered protection characteristic of true vocal folds.
notes.E: Stratified columnar epithelium is not the characteristic protective epithelial lining over the vibrating surfaces of true vocal folds.

questions.stem: The cartilage of the epiglottis is:
questions.why: The epiglottis contains elastic cartilage, whose abundant elastic fibres allow flexible deformation and recoil. Its cartilage core helps support the epiglottic structure during swallowing without the rigidity of typical hyaline cartilage.

notes.A: Hyaline cartilage supports structures including tracheal rings and much of the laryngeal framework, rather than the flexible epiglottis.
notes.C: Fibrocartilage contains dense collagen bundles adapted to tensile and compressive loading, unlike the elastic cartilage core of the epiglottis.
notes.D: Calcified hyaline cartilage may occur in ageing laryngeal structures, but the epiglottis normally consists of elastic cartilage.
notes.E: Articular cartilage covers synovial joint surfaces and is not the characteristic cartilage forming the flexible epiglottic framework.

questions.stem: The open ends of the tracheal cartilages are joined posteriorly by:
questions.why: C-shaped hyaline tracheal rings are incomplete posteriorly, where the trachealis smooth muscle spans their open ends. Contraction narrows the tracheal lumen, while the posterior arrangement accommodates oesophageal distension during swallowing.

notes.A: Cricopharyngeus forms part of the upper oesophageal sphincter and is not the posterior smooth muscle connecting tracheal rings.
notes.B: Fibroelastic connective tissue contributes to the posterior wall, but trachealis smooth muscle directly spans the open cartilaginous ends.
notes.D: The oesophagus lies posterior to the trachea but does not itself form the muscular connection between tracheal cartilage ends.
notes.E: Tracheal cartilage is hyaline, and the posterior gap is bridged by fibroelastic tissue and smooth muscle rather than elastic cartilage.

questions.stem: The basement membrane under the tracheal epithelium is notably:
questions.why: The tracheal respiratory epithelium rests on a conspicuous basement membrane region, often appearing thick in routine histological sections. It separates the epithelial lining from underlying lamina propria and provides structural support.

notes.A: The tracheal epithelium possesses a basal lamina and associated extracellular matrix rather than lacking a basement membrane region.
notes.B: Fenestrations are characteristic of selected endothelial capillaries, not the normal basement membrane beneath tracheal respiratory epithelium.
notes.C: Calcification may affect ageing tracheal cartilage but is not the usual appearance of the epithelial basement membrane.
notes.E: The epithelial basement membrane is normally continuous and provides an interface between tracheal epithelial cells and lamina propria.

questions.stem: Bronchioles are distinguished from bronchi by:
questions.why: Bronchioles lack cartilage plates and submucosal glands, unlike bronchi. Their walls contain smooth muscle and progressively simpler epithelium, with club cells becoming prominent in smaller conducting bronchioles.

notes.A: C-shaped hyaline rings identify the trachea or major extrapulmonary airways, rather than the cartilage-free walls of bronchioles.
notes.B: Seromucous glands occur in bronchial submucosa, whereas bronchioles lack these glands and rely on epithelial secretory cells.
notes.C: Bronchioles lack the organised gland-bearing submucosal compartment typical of larger bronchi, rather than possessing an especially thick one.
notes.D: Bronchiolar lining becomes simple columnar or cuboidal distally, rather than being distinguished by stratified epithelium.

questions.stem: Asthma narrows the airways mainly by contraction of smooth muscle in the:
questions.why: Asthma involves variable airway narrowing from smooth-muscle contraction, inflammation and mucus accumulation. Bronchi and bronchioles both contribute, with narrowing of small conducting airways particularly increasing resistance to airflow.

notes.B: Tracheal smooth muscle can alter airway diameter, but asthma characteristically involves widespread bronchial and bronchiolar obstruction rather than isolated tracheal narrowing.
notes.C: Laryngeal narrowing causes upper-airway obstruction and may mimic asthma, but is not its characteristic intrapulmonary mechanism.
notes.D: Alveolar ducts contain limited smooth muscle around alveolar openings, rather than the prominent contractile airway coats implicated in asthma.
notes.E: Nasal obstruction may accompany allergic disease, but asthma primarily affects lower intrapulmonary conducting airways rather than nasal passages.

questions.stem: Club (Clara) cells are mainly found in the:
questions.why: Club cells are non-ciliated secretory epithelial cells especially abundant in terminal bronchioles. They produce protective secretory proteins, participate in xenobiotic metabolism and can contribute to renewal of bronchiolar epithelium.

notes.A: Tracheal epithelium predominantly contains ciliated, goblet and basal cells, rather than being the principal location of club cells.
notes.C: Main bronchial epithelium contains ciliated and mucus-secreting populations; club cells become especially prominent in smaller bronchioles.
notes.D: Alveolar sacs are lined mainly by type I and type II pneumocytes, rather than the bronchiolar club-cell population.
notes.E: The larynx contains respiratory and stratified squamous epithelial regions, not the principal bronchiolar site of club cells.

questions.stem: Most of the alveolar surface is covered by:
questions.why: Type I pneumocytes are extremely flattened alveolar epithelial cells covering approximately 95% of alveolar surface area. Their thin cytoplasm provides a short diffusion pathway between air and pulmonary capillary blood.

notes.A: Type II pneumocytes are cuboidal secretory cells and occupy considerably less alveolar surface area despite their important surfactant function.
notes.B: Alveolar macrophages migrate over alveolar surfaces and remove debris but do not form the continuous epithelial lining.
notes.D: Club cells primarily line bronchioles rather than covering the extensive squamous gas-exchange surface of alveoli.
notes.E: Brush cells are specialised chemosensory epithelial cells, not the principal flattened cells lining alveolar gas-exchange surfaces.

questions.stem: Lamellar bodies seen in alveolar cells contain:
questions.why: Lamellar bodies are membrane-bound secretory organelles in type II pneumocytes that store pulmonary surfactant. Their concentric lipid-rich lamellae are released into alveolar lining fluid, lowering surface tension.

notes.A: Mucins are stored in secretory granules of goblet cells and glands, rather than the surfactant-rich lamellar bodies of pneumocytes.
notes.B: Alveolar macrophage lysosomes degrade phagocytosed particles; lamellar bodies in type II cells primarily store surfactant material.
notes.C: Haemosiderin is an iron-storage pigment accumulating in macrophages after erythrocyte breakdown, rather than normal surfactant-containing lamellar bodies.
notes.E: Odorant-binding proteins participate in olfactory mucosal function and are unrelated to pulmonary type II cell surfactant organelles.

questions.stem: After alveolar injury, the cells that divide to restore the lining are:
questions.why: Type II pneumocytes retain proliferative capacity and can generate replacement type II and type I alveolar epithelial cells following injury. This regenerative function complements their role in synthesising pulmonary surfactant.

notes.A: Mature type I pneumocytes are highly specialised flattened gas-exchange cells with limited conventional proliferative capacity compared with type II cells.
notes.B: Alveolar macrophages remove debris and regulate inflammation but do not normally regenerate the epithelial lining as its principal progenitors.
notes.C: Bronchial basal cells renew conducting airway epithelium, whereas type II pneumocytes are the major local alveolar epithelial progenitors.
notes.D: Endothelial cells restore vascular lining after injury, rather than serving as the principal source of replacement alveolar epithelial cells.

questions.stem: "Heart failure cells" in the lung are:

options.label: B
options.text: type II cells full of surfactant

options.label: D
options.text: club cells that have lost cilia

questions.why: Pulmonary venous congestion can cause erythrocytes to leak into alveolar spaces, where macrophages ingest them. Iron from haemoglobin accumulates as haemosiderin, creating the pigment-laden macrophages classically called heart failure cells.

notes.B: Type II pneumocytes contain surfactant-rich lamellar bodies, not the characteristic iron pigment accumulated after erythrocyte phagocytosis.
notes.C: Neutrophils participate in acute inflammation but are not the characteristic long-lived haemosiderin-containing alveolar phagocytes of chronic congestion.
notes.D: Club cells are normally non-ciliated bronchiolar secretory cells and do not account for haemosiderin accumulation within alveolar macrophages.
notes.E: Erythrocytes in capillaries are a normal finding; heart failure cells are macrophages containing iron derived from degraded erythrocytes.

questions.stem: The thinnest part of the blood–air barrier is formed where:

options.label: A
options.text: type II cells overlie the capillary

options.label: B
options.text: type I cell and endothelial basal laminae fuse

options.label: E
options.text: club cells line the alveolar duct

questions.why: The thinnest gas-exchange region occurs where flattened type I pneumocytes closely oppose capillary endothelium and their basal laminae fuse. This arrangement minimises interstitial tissue and shortens the diffusion pathway for respiratory gases.

notes.A: Cuboidal type II pneumocytes are thicker than type I cells and principally support surfactant production rather than minimal diffusion distance.
notes.C: Macrophage migration across alveolar tissues participates in immune defence, not formation of the thinnest structural gas-exchange barrier.
notes.D: Fibroblast-containing septal interstitium increases separation between epithelial and endothelial layers, producing thicker rather than thinnest barrier regions.
notes.E: Club cells primarily occur in bronchiolar epithelium and do not form the thin squamous alveolar gas-exchange barrier.

questions.stem: Pores of Kohn are important clinically because they:

options.label: C
options.text: allow infection to spread between alveoli

questions.why: Pores of Kohn are small communications between adjacent alveoli that permit collateral ventilation and pressure equilibration. These same openings can allow inflammatory exudate and microorganisms to spread through neighbouring airspaces.

notes.A: Type II pneumocytes synthesise surfactant; interalveolar pores are structural openings rather than specialised surfactant-producing cells.
notes.B: Alveolar macrophages phagocytose inhaled dust, whereas pores of Kohn permit communication between neighbouring alveolar airspaces.
notes.D: Pulmonary lymphatics drain interstitial tissue fluid, while pores of Kohn connect airspaces rather than forming lymphatic drainage channels.
notes.E: Surfactant is the principal surface-active mechanism preventing alveolar collapse; interalveolar pores primarily provide collateral communication.

questions.stem: Lobar bronchi correspond to which airway generation?
questions.why: In the classical Weibel branching model, the trachea is generation zero, main bronchi generation one and lobar bronchi generation two. Real airway branching is asymmetric, so generation numbers are approximate anatomical landmarks.

notes.A: Generation zero corresponds to the trachea, before its division into the right and left main bronchi.
notes.B: Generation ten represents much more distal branching in the idealised model, rather than the initial lobar bronchi.
notes.C: Generations eleven through sixteen encompass distal conducting branches, far beyond the second-generation lobar bronchi in this model.
notes.E: Generation twenty-three represents the terminal alveolar region of the idealised branching model, rather than proximal lobar conducting bronchi.

questions.stem: The nasal vestibule is distinguished by:
questions.why: The anterior nasal vestibule is a skin-lined region containing keratinised stratified squamous epithelium, hairs called vibrissae and cutaneous glands. Vibrissae intercept relatively large inhaled particles before air reaches deeper respiratory mucosa.

notes.A: Olfactory sensory neurons and Bowman's glands occupy specialised superior nasal mucosa rather than the skin-lined anterior vestibule.
notes.B: Large venous plexuses are prominent within respiratory nasal mucosa, rather than being the defining histological feature of the vestibule.
notes.C: Ciliated respiratory epithelium replaces the skin-like vestibular lining more posteriorly, where mucociliary conditioning of inspired air becomes prominent.
notes.D: Elastic cartilage and seromucous glands do not identify the cutaneous vestibule, whose hallmark is squamous lining with coarse hairs.

questions.stem: Inspired air is warmed in the conducting airways mainly by the:

options.label: A
options.text: vascular bed of the lamina propria

options.label: D
options.text: elastic fibres of the airway wall

questions.why: A rich vascular network beneath conducting airway epithelium transfers heat from circulating blood to inspired air. Nasal mucosal vessels are especially important for warming air before it reaches the delicate lower respiratory passages.

notes.B: Seromucous glands contribute moisture and mucus, but heat transfer chiefly depends on blood perfusing the underlying mucosal vascular bed.
notes.C: Ciliary beating transports mucus towards the pharynx rather than generating the principal heat exchange needed to warm inspired air.
notes.D: Elastic fibres provide structural recoil and support to airway walls, rather than acting as the main source of transferred heat.
notes.E: Hyaline cartilage maintains airway patency but is not the richly perfused structure responsible for warming inspired air.

questions.stem: Immune protection in the airway lamina propria is provided by:

options.label: E
options.text: type I pneumocytes of the wall

questions.why: Bronchus-associated lymphoid tissue comprises organised or diffuse mucosal immune cells associated with airways, particularly after antigenic stimulation. These lymphocytes and antigen-presenting cells contribute to local immune surveillance and respiratory mucosal defence.

notes.A: Kupffer cells are resident macrophages of hepatic sinusoids, not the organised lymphoid tissue associated with respiratory airways.
notes.C: Peyer's patches are aggregated lymphoid nodules in the small intestine, rather than the characteristic airway-associated lymphoid tissue.
